En estos útimos dias no sólo se vió afectada gran cantidad de flora y fauna nativa, sino también los incendios llegaron a los conglomerados urbanos 🏠, lo que hizo que algunas familias tuvieran que abandonar sus viviendas por la cercanía del 🔥. "Uno de los videos compartidos muestra a yacarés mientras se mueven en grupo a través de un camino de tierra. Y agregó: <Son una de las tantas especies que hoy se ven obligados a dejar sus ambientes naturales. Por otro lado también tenemos ejemplares con quemadura graves>.⁠

For decades, scientists have warned that the Amazon rainforest might reach a critical tipping point, irreversibly transitioning to a drier, savanna-like ecosystem. Now, a new study shows that 75% of the rainforest has lost resilience—that means it can’t bounce back or recover as quickly after droughts and human disturbance.

The Amazon has endured changes in rainfall throughout history, but large-scale deforestation, drought, and fires—all fueled by climate change—are threatening the very processes that make it a rainforest. Scientists say this will have negative consequences for people and wildlife, including the more than 1,500 bird species that call it home.

“This study tells us something about the actual world we live in,” says Chris Boulton, who led the study’s team of researchers. But despite these concerning findings, Chris believes there’s still hope. “It gives people a chance to do something about it potentially.”

O magnésio vem sendo estudado em diversas patologias como doenças cardiovasculares, doenças autoimunes, em nutrição esportiva e diversas aplicações na saúde da mulher.
É um mineral eficaz na prevenção da dismenorréia, síndrome pré-menstrual e enxaqueca menstrual e na prevenção de sintomas do climatério.
Também parece haver uma conexão entre baixos teores de magnésio, zinco e ferro e a maior incidência de sintomas depressivos, alterações de humor e cognição na menopausa.
Princialmente mulheres na pós-menopausa deve dar mais atenção a esses micronutrientes.

Fontes alimentares de magnésio: cereais integrais, nabo, couve, espinafre, aipo, pepino, feijão-verde, banana, damasco, abacate, pêssego, ameixa, maçã, nozes, amêndoas, caju, amendoim, sementes de abóbora e girassol, cacau, batatas e peixes como linguado, cavala, salmão.
As fontes alimentares são diversas e abundantes, facilitando a introdução deste mineral por meio da alimentação.

Posted @xxx • @xxx A menopausa é um acontecimento natural na vida da mulher, definida como a cessação da menstruação por doze meses consecutivos.
E por que se fala tanto da menopausa se ela é um acontecimento natural?
Com a chegada da menopausa e a queda de hormônios muitas mudanças acontecem no corpo da mulher, predispondo o aparecimento de sintomas e a ocorrência de doenças.

Por isso a importância de tomar alguns cuidados antes dela chegar como manter peso adequado, alimentação saudável, rica em cálcio e vitamina D e pobre em gorduras saturadas, evitar cigarro e consumo excessivo de álcool e fazer exercícios regularmente (musculação, exercícios com sobrecarga de peso, de flexibilidade e equilíbrio)...
Além destas medidas gerais, o tratamento de reposição hormonal é indicado para minimizar os sintomas que a diminuição dos hormônios traz e diminuir alguns riscos de complicações de saúde.

Muitas vezes os sintomas, como fogachos, suores noturnos, redução do desejo sexual, alterações o humor são bastante incômodos e interferem com a qualidade de vida nessa fase. Por isso, apesar da menopausa ser um acontecimento natural, o acompanhamento com ginecologista é tão importante.

A recuperação do estresse crônico e da disfunção adrenal envolve uma abordagem multidisciplinar: abordar as fontes de inflamação, equilibrar o açúcar no sangue, comer uma dieta rica em nutrientes, sono adequado e práticas consistentes de redução do estresse (como exercício físico).
Uma vez que tenhamos essas bases no lugar, podemos usar ervas e suplementos para aumentar ainda mais nossa capacidade de gerenciar o estresse e acelerar nossa recuperação.
Aqui estão alguns dos meus favoritos (verifique com seu médico antes de iniciar uma nova erva ou suplemento):
➔ Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) demonstrou reduzir o estresse e a ansiedade ocasional.
A dosagem terapêutica está na faixa de 200-400 mg por dia.

➔ Erva-cidreira. A erva-cidreira pode reduzir os sentimentos de estresse e ansiedade, tornando o neurotransmissor (GABA) mais facilmente acessível no cérebro. O GABA ajuda a regular a resposta ao estresse do seu corpo.
➔ Manjericão (Tulsi) Estudos científicos mostraram que o tulsi pode potencialmente combater o estresse metabólico através da estabilização dos níveis de glicose no sangue.
➔ L-Theanine, demonstrou inibir a excitação dos neurônios corticais e reduzir a resposta simpática em momentos de alto estresse.
A dosagem é de 100-300 mg, duas a três vezes ao dia.
➔ Rhodiola (Rhodiola Rosea) parece ser capaz de reduzir significativamente a fadiga e 'burnout' que vêm da exposição crônica ao estresse.

We have spent every evening so far of 2022 on the beach, and that pleases me so much. One thing I've noticed is along the seaweed lines or tide lines there are small pieces of plastics and microplastics every couple of inches. At first it looks like shells or sea glass but is always plastic. This is just what is visible to the naked eye, assuming there are far more smaller pieces. What's extra sad is this isn't from beach litter, it is mostly what gets washed up from the ocean. As of 2007, at least 44% of marine bird species ingest plastic. While harder to study, it is hypothesized that all levels of the food chain in the ocean are consuming large amounts of plastic now. That means we are too, it we consume ocean products. So, seriously, reduce the amount of single use plastic you use. Absolutely stop using plastic water bottles. That's the low hanging fruit and if you can't do that then YOU are the problem. Stop using plastic shopping bags. That's more low hanging fruit. It's not going to solve this plastic crisis but it's going to help and it's EASY. All marine animals, and those that rely on marine animals for livelihood and food sources, thank you 😅🌎🐢 🕊️ 🍣 #clawhands #theclaw #noplastic #refuse #sustainability #nosingleuse #plasticfree #zerowaste

Forever Summer is currently in full bloom!⁣

Over the past year we've been working on the development of a new proces based work as well as taking care of around thirty different tomato varieties together with a community. The work has become an ecosystemic installation that circles around the question what happens when you introduce the tomato in the domain of a museum. ⁣

Anyone who has grown tomatoes before, knows that a successful harvest and good yield correlates with a good summer. Despite the seasons it seems that the supermarket always provides us with a ‘good summer’. Fresh products are offered all year round because we are able to control the atmosphere. A permanent summer is formed by the ratio between oxygen, nitrogen and CO2, temperature and preservatives like E200 and E299. This system brings all year long summertime into our households.⁣

The Van Abbemuseum and the depot are climate controlled spaces as well. 18°C and a humidity of around 60% is what it takes to present and conserve art. A temperature and humidity similar to greenhouses for growing tomatoes. What happens when the tomatoes become part of the collection of the museum? ⁣

Advantages of planting trees in reducing global warming.
* An average size tree creates sufficient oxygen in one year to provide oxygen for a family of four.
* Planting trees can cut air-conditioning/ electricity costs up to 50 percent.
* Planting trees for the environment is good as they are renewable, biodegradable and recyclable.
* If we plant 20 million trees, the earth will get 260 million more tons of oxygen.
* One acre of trees can remove up to 2.6 tons of Carbon Dioxide each year.
* During photosynthesis, trees and other plants absorb carbon dioxide and give off oxygen.
* Trees keep in check the air and water pollution.
* Why planting trees is important is evident as they are the natural habitat of the animals and birds, as well as many endangered species.
* Planting trees means more wood and paper products which can be easily recycled.
* A newly planted whole forest can change tones of atmospheric carbon into wood and other fibrous tissue, thus reducing global warming.

There is a lot to love about the outward strength and resilience of a mature tree... but is there more to these grand earth dwellers.?
"Trees look after their own, help their sick and are even reluctant to abandon their dead" .. these are the findings of scientists researching the sensitivity and interconnectedness of trees.
Walk into any forest and you will instantly feel it.. but will we ever really know the language of these great 'ancestors'.

For me it's a language that is something greater than words.. an unseen support system of threads that connect a forest of trees in support of each other..sharing resources by emitting distress chemicals, and sending messages or nutrients through underground mycorrhizal networks.

It is this fascinating communication and support system that earns them my respect and leads me to believe, as I sit here in the soft moss and dappled shadows below a grand old lady, that trees truly are all-knowing ... It is something that has become my focus this week in expressing a sense of it, using paint and paper.

Our world is in what seems like constant development. There seems to be relentless pressure to innovate and to ‘level up’. Some of this pressure comes from our ingenuity and curiosity as a species but a lot comes from capitalist endeavour, always looking to do one better than our closest competitor(rival). 💰

The majors problem with this approach is that our planet only has enough resources to go so far. Once they are depleted they are gone. It would seem that, based on COP26, government’s and lobbyist are keen to wring the very last of our resources unsustainably for a quick buck. 💲

If we lived in a circular economy which embraced reuse and recycle then a more sustainable economy would develop. We would not waste. There would be more to go around and our planet would be a healthier place. 🌍

Is it a quick fix? Certainly not! It’s going to require something from all over us to shift a global economy so dramatically. The rich are currently the most powerful but they are a minority. We must buy sustainably, we must vote green! 💚

What could your role in the climate movement be?

I recently saw this Venn diagram reemerge when @xxx shared it and want to encourage everyone to go through this process to find the intersection of what’s needed, what you’re good at and - most importantly - what brings you joy.

I have personally experienced burn-out because I was focusing on things that I’m good at + are important, but don’t bring me a lot of joy (= organising actions, which many activists love but I find draining). It is important to remember that there’s a role for everyone, and it’s not your responsibility to do something just because you’re good at it. It leads to over-commitment, stress, and not doing any of your roles justice.

Joy is so important for activists. Our work can be dark, difficult and demanding. But it can also be incredibly rewarding when we see the change we’re creating in the here and now. But in order to make our advocacy sustainable, the process - not just the outcome - must be a source of joy.
I’ve also included some slides from a great post by @xxx with some roles that are urgently needed, but not everyone always thinks about. Swipe through!
I would LOVE to hear (and see!) from other people who have gone through this process and what you found that the heart of your diagram 💙

Our earth is pretty amazing! And it has the capacity and capability to provide for and home all of us!
However, under our current broken systems and with the greed we’ve been operating with, we are threatening its ability to do that.

Even if you just grow a bit of basil for yourself, or start a compost bin for your food scraps, that IS a positive change, that IS eliminating food turning into waste (its only waste when its wasted), that IS empowering.

There is nothing better in my mind than finding an allotment site on a canal side in the Brecon Beacons and sneaking in to take some snaps!!
But these places are more than just bits of land and sheds. They’re community hubs, therapy rooms, carbon sequesters. Places to meet, to sit, to grow. To feel safe in.
They’re precious microcosms of the community that surrounds them.

As I snuck through two ladies were deep in conversation but looked up and smiled, and said how precious the space was for them, that they popped across at 11 every day they could for a coffee and a chat with whoever was about!!
And yet we see so many allotment sites at risk.

They’re a reminder to me always that community exists, and that they can be spaces for change. Spaces where people learn about the land, about their food, and how growing food takes skill and understanding and how important it is to pass those skills to our children and children’s children.
Allotments could be the start of the revolution!!!

David Hondula recently got a job he never dreamed of—maybe because it never existed before.
He’s the director of the @xxx Office of Heat Response & Mitigation, which is touted as the first publicly funded municipal office of its kind.

Sponge City = An urban landscape designed to retain and filter water.

You know the drill: climate change and urbanization are leading to increases in both water shortages and flooding. “Sponge City” is a charming and apt metaphor for how we can reengineer our cities to help regulate the water cycle.
The term was coined by Kongjian Yu, a professor at Peking University and the founder of the Beijing design firm Turenscape. His designs incorporate wetlands to collect, filter, and store stormwater.

Yesterday someone asked me why I wasn’t at a march in  a very angry way, and told me I couldn’t call myself a climate or environmental or food or social or anything activist because I wasn’t at a march………

Now first of all protest is a human right, and I am grateful to every single human who went out yesterday and demanded better and stood up for the planet. It’s so great to see families protesting together, young people, older people, kids and for protest to be something we commit to as families. Teaching kids that protesting, marching, being activists is perfectly normal is awesome when we see our media  being divisive about protests. I was fortunate to have that but I’m pretty sure none of my peers did!!

But then, don’t judge. Let’s remember we’re still in a pandemic where the inequalities of health are still showing up and still the most vulnerable are at risk of serious disease and death. I’ve lived with that now for 18 months. The constant fear of bringing something home to infect Mr V, the constant barrage of news, the failing messages and actions of politicians, the fear of a need to rely on a stretched NHS when already they’ve saved us both, many times.

Judgementalism is the scourge of our age. It takes no account of the intersectionality of lives. It assumes that not only are we all in the same storm, but that we are all in the luxury suite of a cruise liner sailing through it, and ignores that anyone might be in the life rafts, struggling to survive in the wake of their arrogance.
So just a reminder-check your privilege before you berate others for not having the same privilege as you.
And in the meantime here I am, hiding behind a dahlia that’s as big as my head!!

"What you do makes a difference, and you have to decide what kind of difference you want to make" — Dr Jane Goodall. 🙌⁠

From her decades studying chimpanzees in the Gombe forest to her more recent years advocating for the protection of nature & animals, and inspiring youth through her initiative "roots & shoots" the legendary primatologist has always been a hero. ⁠

As we all grapple with the gross injustices against other animals, the destruction of nature for profit, public health crises and the reality of climate change, the world can certainly feel overwhelming. ⁠
Jane's wise & compassionate voice is one we often turn to and her message that every single one of us makes an impact on the planet every single day is an empowering one that rings true. 🙏⁠

Jane is also one of the few voices calling for us to look at the true source of Covid-19 & other zoonotic diseases, and to recognise the reality that - zoonotic diseases spilling over to humans are coming from our exploitation and disrespect of nature & animals. ⁠
A lifelong vegetarian, and recent vegan, Jane wouldn’t say everyone has to be vegan, but says: “If we don’t stop factory farming, we’ve had it.”⁠
In her new book, the Book of Hope: A Survival Guide for Trying Times, Goodall admits to feeling, on many days, as if she’s fighting a losing battle against greed, corruption and prejudice. ⁠
Then there’s a voice that says: "There is still an awful lot left and that’s what we’ve got to fight to save... I’m not going to give in. I’ll die fighting, that’s for sure.” ⁠
And we are with you 100% Jane ✊❤️✌️⁠

7 days, 9 bags of garbage, and still millions more yet to be bagged, out of place in nature.

I originally joined the outdoor education industry because I felt nature conservation and climate change were the world's most pressing issues. I searched for my purpose in life, and I found it despite the pressures of modern society, I wanted to become a voice for this cause.

I often feel conflicted in my position, influencing people to get out and explore nature, knowing that not all will respect the land like many of us do. Every time I lead, I do so with the intent of teaching people how to take care of both themselves, and the wilderness we visit. Except we are not visitors, we are nature, and nature is us.

It's no secret we must continue to reflect on the way we impact these spaces, and how our daily habits influence climate change and the destruction of nature. We can blame the few industries and corporations that contribute the majority of pollution to our planet all we want, but we must remember that we the consumers, are the driving force behind these businesses. Our demand for fast, cheap, and infinite consumption is what keeps this domino effect in motion.

That being said, there are many barriers in place that do not allow everyone the privilege of making these conscious choices, and that's why these changes ultimately must begin at a legislative level. We must appoint diverse leaders who value environmental health and longevity over short-term economic gains at the expense of our planet and every species who call it home. We need people who will not bow to monopolies and lobbyists alike, handing them licenses to kill the Earth without repercussions. Someone who will work for the people and the planet in unison.

It's a complicated issue trying to balance the needs of the modern world in a sustainable fashion, but either way it will begin and end with us. So get out there and pick up some trash, educate and raise children with these values in mind, do however much or little you can. Every army needs a diversified approach with all hands on deck, fighting from all angles. It's not our responsibility as individuals, but as a collective for a better future.

We can stop wasting time debating with climate deniers.
A recent survey from Cornell University, based on 90,000 climate-related studies, has concluded that 99.9% of scientists now agree that humans are altering the climate.
The degree of scientific certainty is now the same as the level of agreement on evolution.
This means there is no doubt among experts that burning fossil fuels, such as oil, gas, coal, peat and trees, is heating the planet and causing more extreme weather.
The survey of peer-reviewed literature published from 2012 to November 2020 was conducted in two stages:
First, the researchers examined a random sample of 3,000 studies, in which they found only found four papers that were sceptical that the climate crisis was caused by humans.

Second, they searched the full database of 88,125 studies for keywords linked to climate scepticism such as “natural cycles” and “cosmic rays”, which yielded 28 papers, all published in minor journals.
The authors said their study, published on Tuesday in the journal Environmental Research Letters, showed scepticism among experts is now vanishingly small.

“It is really case closed. There is nobody of significance in the scientific community who doubts human-caused climate change,” said the lead author, Mark Lynas, a visiting fellow at Cornell University.

The world’s largest plant capturing carbon directly from the air has just started operating in Iceland 😮
It uses direct air capture technology and will capture 4,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year by storing the carbon below ground in basalt rock where it can be mineralised.
This is the process where the air-captured CO2 is mixed with water and pumped deep underground, then trapped in stone through a natural process that takes less than two years 🤓
The plant runs fully on renewable energy, has a small physical footprint and doesn't compete with agriculture for land 👣

While this is for sure a great and exiting invention, it just operates on a small scale yet and does not mean we found a solution for reversing climate change. Reducing our individual carbon footprints is still key to save the planet and live our healthiest life! ✨

A Pegada de Carbono é um índice que mede a quantidade total das emissões de Gases do Efeito Estufa (GEE) - convertido em dióxido de carbono (CO2) - causadas diretamente e indiretamente por uma pessoa, organização, evento ou produto.
Ao calcularmos a nossa pegada de carbono, é possível observar com mais clareza os impactos que nossas ações cotidianas e nossos hábitos de consumo possuem nas mudanças climáticas.

Devido às emissões antropogênicas (liberadas por atividades humanas), as concentrações de CO2 estão aumentando rapidamente. A principal consequência deste aumento da concentração de carbono na atmosfera são as mudanças climáticas.
A boa notícia é que reduzi-la é mais simples do que parece. A mudança de hábitos cotidianos e as pequenas decisões que tomamos contribuem para baixar essa conta.
- Reutilize, recicle e compre materiais reciclados;
- Escolha produtos que possuem embalagens recicláveis ou recicladas;
- Repense sua alimentação, preferindo alimentos orgânicos;
Além disso, existem empresas e sites especializados no cálculo da pegada de carbono, com indicativos de quantas árvores devem ser plantadas para compensar as suas emissões.
É nosso dever como cidadão também pressionar gestores públicos e privados para que essa preocupação também seja prioridade nas esferas públicas, empresarial e industrial.

Dorothy Stang chegou ao Brasil nos anos 1970 para realizar trabalhos pastorais na região amazônica. Sua atuação focou projetos de reflorestamento e de geração de emprego e renda para a população pobre local.⠀

Dorothy stang arrived in Brazil in the 1970s to carry out pastoral work in the amazon region. Advantages of planting trees in reducing global warming.
* An average size tree creates sufficient oxygen in one year to provide oxygen for a family of four.
* Planting trees can cut air-conditioning/ electricity costs up to 50 percent.
* Planting trees for the environment is good as they are renewable, biodegradable and recyclable.
* If we plant 20 million trees, the earth will get 260 million more tons of oxygen.
* One acre of trees can remove up to 2.6 tons of Carbon Dioxide each year.
* During photosynthesis, trees and other plants absorb carbon dioxide and give off oxygen.
* Trees keep in check the air and water pollution.
* Why planting trees is important is evident as they are the natural habitat of the animals and birds, as well as many endangered species.
* Planting trees means more wood and paper products which can be easily recycled.
* A newly planted whole forest can change tones of atmospheric carbon into wood and other fibrous tissue, thus reducing global warming.

We can all do this, together!

BVN is honoured to have been awarded Climate Active certification in acknowledgement of our commitment to sustainability. This is a big win for us as a practice, as well as for our projects, our collaborators, our people and our environments. We join a global network of organisations with a shared commitment to real and authentic decision making about treading lightly on the earth. Our industry is pivotal to sustainability action and we are proud to become an official Climate Active Organisation.
BVN’s commitment to sustainability is part of our collective vision, to strive daily to be SMARTER, MORE CREATIVE & BETTER FOR THE PLANET.
It’s a commitment that extends both inside and outside our organisation. How we run our studios. How we travel to work. How we design our buildings. How we choose our suppliers.
So what exactly does Climate Active certification mean?
Well, it’s a standard based on a sustainability audit of company operations. That means energy supply, waste management, food and beverage provisions, even the way we get around.
Climate Active certification is recognised as one of the most rigorous standards in the world.
For BVN, holding this certification means making decisions every day about how we work, through the lens of our environmental impact.
"It is not enough to do less harm – we have to aim to leave the planet in a BETTER state that we found it” says Neil Logan, Co-CEO of BVN.
“Our actions have to be aimed at regenerating the planet and this starts with getting our own house in order.
We are aiming for better than climate neutral. We’re aiming for ‘climate positive’. Securing Climate Active Certification has been crucial to this process."
This is just the start of our journey. We invite you to follow us as we share our learnings, our experiments, our dilemmas and our successes. Perhaps you’ll be inspired too.

It's estimated that by 2030 synthetic fibres will represent 73% of fibre production, of which 85% will be polyester. Polyester is made from non-renewable fossil fuels such as crude oil and natural gas, so when you buy a garment with polyester in, fossil fuel extraction has occurred for you to wear it.

“Synthetics Anonymous: Fashion brands’ addiction to fossil fuels” (link in bio) by @xxx exposes how increased use of synthetic fibres is allowing brands to sell big volumes of cheap, disposable clothes. Greenwashing is fuelling this addiction to fossil-fuel based clothing as it distracts consumers from the truth and provides a false reassurance about shopping.

Some brands have adopted recycled polyester whilst continuing to push synthetic fibres alongside their ‘eco-friendly’ recycled collection. However in reality, recycled polyester requires more energy to process than cotton, wool or hemp and does nothing to resolve the serious issue of shedding microplastics. Brands like @xxx and @xxx advertise their use of ocean plastics as an ‘eco-innovative replacement’ for virgin plastic, but the current volumes of extraction of ocean plastic for this use are miniscule and all these materials do is shed plastics each time we wash them.

Recycled synthetic clothing feels like a false solution and a far cry from the circular model that fashion needs to adopt. I can’t help but feel that attempting to make synthetic fibres palatable under the ‘recycled’ or ‘ocean plastic’ banner is a lazy attempt at sustainability. Brands taking this approach aren’t doing anything to address a dependence on fossil-fuel based fibres. Surely they need to carve out a better future for fashion based on natural materials that can be grown regeneratively and returned to the soil in a #climatepositive way?

For a down to earth dose of circularity and regenerative fashion, the @xxx starts tomorrow @xxx . The main exhibition features Indian fibres showcasing the production cycle from seed to clothing and I’m heading there on Sunday to be part of a panel discussion about British fibres.

Did you know that a quarter of front gardens are totally paved over?
Removing even a few paving stones and replacing them with perennial plants grown to maturity is one way to take climate-positive action at home.
Replacing 1m² of paving with herbaceous perennials (lawn grasses
and non-woody plants) can draw 3.21kg carbon/m² out of the air!

The ultimate symbol of wealth, the super-yacht has seen a dramatic surge in demand during the pandemic, as the ultra-rich yearned for privacy and social distancing in its most luxurious, exclusive form.
Large super-yachts have a disproportionately negative impact on the planet.
According to one calculation by Indiana University anthropologists, one with a permanent crew, a helicopter pad, submarines and pools emits over 7,000 tons of CO2 a year.

Multiplied by 300, roughly the number of superyachts worldwide that fit that bill that equals over 2 million tons of CO2, more than the individual yearly emissions of about a quarter of the world's countries.

Now, a proposed ship aims to leverage the superyacht's aura of luxury and merge it with scientific research to create an emissions-free mega-ship that will pit together climate scientists and the wealthy in a daring quest to save the planet.

If built, the new vessel, to be christened Earth 300 in reference to its length of 300 meters, or 984 feet, would dwarf even the world's largest super-yacht, the 590-foot long Azzam, owned by the Abu Dhabi royal family.

The preliminary design is sleek and bold, with a unique 13-story sphere that will house two dozen scientific laboratories. They will gather data from the ship's travels to hopefully come up with solutions to help mitigate the climate crisis.
Most of the ship's capacity of 425 people will be taken up by two main groups: 165 crew and 160 scientists.

Olivera, who has a background in the world of luxury and hospitality in Singapore, says the inspiration for Earth 300 came when he was diving in the Maldives and saw its dying corals. He envisages the ship as a way of combining two colliding worlds, luxury and environmentalism.

The idea of a luxury research vessel isn't entirely new. REV Ocean, a similar project hailing from Norway, is a 600-foot long, $350 million superyacht designed to investigate overfishing, climate change and plastic pollution.

In an effort to address the effects of climate change, the EU has created the European Climate Pact to share ideas, develop solutions, and learn more about climate change so that we can properly adjust our everyday habits while encouraging wider support of new laws and policies. Hooray 🎉🎉🎉
Whether you’re from the EU or not, this is a great resource for figuring out how to increase your role in creating a greener future!
One of the main focuses is reducing carbon emissions, on both an industrial and individual scale, which will drastically impact the rate at which oceans are warming and becoming acidic.

♻️ Some easy changes you can make include: updating or replacing your electronics less frequently, switching to a more plant-based diet, using public transportation, switching flights for train rides, shopping locally, sending a few less e-mails, and even setting your thermostat a few degrees closer to the temperature outside.
There is no action too small when it comes to slowing climate change, after all there’s 7 billion of us! Let’s see what we can do when we all work together 🙌🏽

Did you know that one bottle of desflurane, an anaesthetic used in surgery, contains carbon equal to a year of eight mile trips by car?
This is not good for the environment. Dr Geraldine Gallagher, an anaesthetist at Glasgow Royal Infirmary, is one staff member making a difference.
We now use less of this gas. In three months, the GRI anaesthetist team have saved CO2 equal to the department's annual commute.
(Image description: Dr Geraldine Gallagher, in her theatre, holding a sign "Climate Change, What Can We Do About It?")
We know that the way we currently grow our food is destroying the planet. We know that intensive agricultural practices are tied to land degradation and desertification.

It’s time to revolutionize our food systems. Regenerative agriculture solutions like the Forest Garden Approach respect the land that produces our food, rather than draining it of its precious natural resources.
The relationship between our food systems and our climate can be renewed to help both people and planet. So let’s get planting!

I recently sat down and had an amazing chat with Giselle Carr from @xxx  and  interior architect, Yutaka Takiura @xxx about natural disasters and how visual artists and designers can play a role in this.  What is our design responsibility and how can we help create more resilient societies?

⚡️The unpredictable nature of weather and climatic disasters has lasting ramifications for nations that experience them. Island nations around the world are susceptible to a multitude of threats, yet are also incredibly resilient and adaptive in their responses to change.

🌏 We have seen this in Japan, in the recovery of the country after 2011’s triple disaster (earthquake, tsunami, Fukushima nuclear crisis) and more recently in St. Vincent and the Grenadines after the eruption and prolonged activity of the Soufrière Volcano in the midst of a global pandemic.

⛰ Some countries are attempting to become “climate resilient”, such as Dominica, by having a multi-layered approach to responding to disasters. Many of the attempts towards “climate resilience” tackle the looming threats of today, and try to create solutions that consider the generations to come.
💭 It begs the question - can resilience be designed? And if so, how do we create it, and what are the parameters to responsibly designing it?
💡In this conversation, we explore the terrain of recovery, of reimagination, and reflect on the ways that cultures around the world have leaned into these experiences.

Recently the Environment Secretary George Eustice announced changes to the regulation of gene edited crop trials for research purposes. We welcome the proposed changes which will allow field trials of genome edited crops, where the genetic changes could have occurred naturally or as a result of traditional breeding methods, to progress without requiring the same level of regulation that applies to genetically modified organisms 🧬

Genome editing can be used to develop new crop varieties, allowing a precise, targeted mutation in the DNA of an organism. This technology could be used to significantly speed up the crop breeding process and help us to make advances in addressing some of the world’s most pressing challenges – climate change, food security and sustainable food production 🌍

Public libraries are critical climate resilience infrastructure 📚📚📚

The public library was one of my favorite places to spend time as a kid, and I probably have the library’s summer reading challenges to thank for my love of books today. However, I didn’t fully appreciate the role that libraries can and do play in cultivating community care, health, connection, and resilience- particularly amidst a changing and chaotic climate- until I read PALACES FOR THE PEOPLE by @xxx (highly recommend!). And I was further convinced when reading the incredible @xxx report RESILIENCE BEFORE DISASTER: THE NEED TO BUILD EQUITABLE, COMMUNITY-DRIVEN SOCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE, which illustrates how existing community spaces, with a bit of savvy, community-led infrastructure development and thoughtful programming, can be transformed into resilience hubs equipped to provide support for disaster response and recovery.

Libraries certainly aren’t the be-all, end-all of social infrastructure, and, like most public spaces, they’re imperfect and can be sites of conflict and discomfort at times. Nonetheless, they’re incredibly valuable and, with proper investment and prioritization, our public libraries could blossom into a robust network of safe spaces and reliable services protecting and connecting communities amidst climate chaos.

If you feel similarly, it’s fortunately pretty easy to support your local library! Since libraries make their case for funding based on patronage stats, get a membership card if you don’t currently have one, rent some books (check out Libby and OverDrive for audiobook and ebook rentals) and get your friends to do the same, attend events/programming, let your local reps know how much your library means to you, and if you have the bandwidth, consider joining your local Friends of the Library or donate some of your time/books!

California is once again experiencing a record breaking fire season. There are four main culprits of the increased frequency and severity of wildfires. The first is climate change, which is causing longer and more frequent droughts. These droughts dry out vegetation which makes fires more likely to ignite, spread faster once they do, and harder to put out. This has led to fire seasons that are now on average 78 days longer than in 1970.

The second culprit is logging. Harvesting the most profitable (largest) trees from the forest leaves behind smaller more flammable trees that burn more quickly and spread fires faster. It opens the forest canopy, allowing drier conditions and more sunlight to increase the growth of brushy vegetation. Harvesting also produced highly flammable slash that acts as kindling during a wildfire. In recent years across the US, fires have burned with the least intensity in areas with the most protections from logging.

The third culprit is how California conducts firefighting. When a forest is starved of fire for too long, fuels can build up which make the eventual fire that does break out more severe. Indigenous Californians have always known this and, prior to European contact, they regularly conducted cultural burns that helped maintain balance.

The final part of the problem is that we’ve continued to expand building homes in the Wildland Urban Interface (WUI). The Wildland Urban Interface is the area where people’s homes begin to encroach into formerly unoccupied areas. California is poised to become the first state to pass sweeping protections to save the world’s dying rainforests through procurement provisions in proposed state projects. The California Deforestation-Free Procurement Act, or AB 416, passed the California Senate with a 30-8 vote and heads now to Gov. Gavin Newsom for approval by Oct. 11. If Newsom signs the bill into law, California will become the first U.S. state to require contracts for state projects to certify that their operations won’t contribute to rainforest deforestation. The bill would apply to all contracts starting Jan. 1, 2024, and would include all wood and wood products harvested from forests on or after Jan. 1, 2022. The legislation comes at a critical time, with many animal and plant species tragically on the verge of extinction due to rapid deforestation. Denouncing deforestation and contracting with companies committed to protecting forests also would have benefits for humans. The bill notes that deforestation causes 20% of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions and that stopping the loss of forests, mangroves and wetlands would improve our climate situation by that same degree. The bill also would add some ‘teeth’ to the procurement process by allowing penalties for contractors who knowingly lie about the source of their wood products — including slapping them with a misdemeanor. Lady Freethinker applauds the nonprofits and legislators pushing for this needed change to combat climate change and save precious rainforests and animals before it is too late.

Look at the #hotbirdinhand we have for you this week! Volunteer seabird research assistant Sarah Hecocks handles a Common Murre as part of her master's study understanding this species' foraging strategies during the chick rearing phase.

#didyouknow? Common Murres are the most abundant breeding seabird in northern and central California.  They nest in very dense colonies on slopes and cliffs. This is why Sarah is wearing a harness for added security because reaching these nests can be precarious #safetyfirst.

Murres have a wild history on the Farallon Islands, once numbering close to 1 million birds prior to the 1850s, but when their eggs were poached to supply Gold Rush San Francisco their population was all but extirpated. With increased ocean and coastal management over the decades, their population has now increased to 250,000 residing birds around the Gulf of the Farallones.

Seabird volunteer research assistants are part of a rigorous training program at Point Blue's field station on Southeast Farallon Island, where they learn to safely monitor seabirds and record data on each bird. The information collected allows us to better understand how populations of birds are doing and in turn gives us insight into the health of the systems we research. Learn more about our seasonal internships by visiting the careers page on our website (link in bio)!

I loved The Overstory. I think something seeped through its pages into my fingers. Messages whispered from the trees they once were. The Overstory made me see the ground beneath my feet differently - the web of mycorrhiza forever revealed to me. If you ask my daughters, it made me a little obsessed with trees. It brought home the power of fiction to make us think & see the world differently.

So, I’d been waiting for this one. And again it shifted my focus, to the creatures that buzz, crawl, hop and fly around us - to most people a background chorus with their necessity and details blurred. Even more so, it shifted my gaze to the sky and all the worlds I’ll never know exist. It somehow put our plant in perspective in terms of our almost impossibly vast and slowly emerging universe and yet it also emphasised its importance and our duty to protect all the tiny essential living things that interact to make our magical home.

I expect anxiety about the way our species treats this planet has kept many of us from sleeping. In my experience this feeling is even stronger in children - their eyes see the injustice of it so clearly. So the father-son relationship with this theme at the core was such an emotive one to explore. I had flashes of the father and son in The Road and I felt that the protagonists in the books could feel us teetering on the brink of a world that might not be too dissimilar to that. Grief was explored beautifully and heart breakingly too in the story of the mother who was missing and yet very much there in so many ways.

This was a fascinating portrait of a father as he  grappled with the idea of medicating his son with Ritalin when he could see the world so much more clearly than those prescribing it in many ways. Not a perfect father, but one full of love. & the alternative they find to medication was an interesting concept to explore.
In short, I loved it. If I’m honest, perhaps not quite as much as The Overstory, but again it shifted my gaze beautifully. Perfect title too. Worthy of the Booker. Do you agree?

Heatwaves kill more people in Australia than any other 'natural' disaster, and things like running fans in a hot room can actually make things worse.
The good news is that heatwave death can mostly be avoided if we know how to prepare.

Things like identifying cooler places to spend the hottest part of the day (be it a friend's place, a creek, or an air conditioned library or mall), and checking on those who live in hotter neighbourhoods or who are more vulnerable to heat stroke can help. A fan in a hot, dry room will send our body temperature soaring, whereas a fan blowing onto wet clothing will cool us. Relying on air conditioning doesn't always work as blackouts are common during heatwaves (partly because electric companies shut down power to avoid fire risk from power lines, and partly because of the increased demand on the grid). Do you know the signs of heat stroke? Do you know what to do if someone is vomiting or passing out?
As we're seeing in North America, heatwaves are becoming more intense and more frequent with climate change, so it pays to make a plan, be prepared, and look out for others in our community.
Let us know in the comments what you do to get through a heatwave.

Yesterday I was asked if there is a template to write to your MP, and whilst many organisations offer templates for specific issues, I couldn’t find a generic one. So I thought it might be useful to share what I write.
First of all, always put your address on any correspondence as if there’s no address they don’t have to acknowledge it!!

Introduce your topic, state your opinions, add any links to scientific research, peer reviewed stuff and campaigns, and sign off. Doesn’t need to be long winded, just needs to introduce the issue, your stance and facts.

What else is important to remember is that most MP’s get their correspondence sifted by an assistant so they very well may not see it but as king as they know you’re their constituent, it has to be logged.
And don’t worry about grammatical correctness-it’s not an exam!!
If you don’t get a response don’t worry. You’ve made your point. Just keep making it. Short, sharp, factual and regular!!

But most of all, we vote for our MPs to represent us and our future generations. Whilst it doesn’t often feel like it, they work for us. Find out a bit about them-what’s their background and who else might they work for, in order to be able to ask them to ensure they’re representing their constituents and not their own agendas or others who pay them.
I hope that helps a bit. Xx

The work began as a light hearted, tragi-comedic study of our relationship with the natural world and how we have packaged and perfected it to our needs and desires. But with our increased understanding of climate breakdown, in a world that we have created (the anthropocene) comes something darker. The images, often everyday details, sometimes humorous, provide us with a much more uncomfortable realisation, and lead us to consider how and why we have got to where we are. Some clues, some evidence. We can stuff a dead animal, put it in a box, we can use nature as camouflage, we can force and control, conquering, sanitising, packaging and perfecting. But as we stare out over the precipice with an increasing sense of unease and fear, we’re confronted with the fact that we’ve exploited and overlooked the natural balance, the natural order. We’re not in control at all. We’ve been kidding ourselves all along.
